steps.message: Reviewing the intake and the question.

claims.text: Goal: cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030 on an $800,000 capital budget (budget year 2027), for an elementary school in the Bronx.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Rooftop solar alone is estimated to cover only about 22% to 24% of annual use, so it does not reach the 30% goal by itself.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency only (Scenario A) does not reach the goal: estimated reduction 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency plus solar within budget (Scenario B) does not clearly reach the goal: the low end of its range is below 30%. Estimated reduction is 28.3% to 41.9%.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full path (Scenario C: deeper efficiency, whole-roof solar and a backup battery) reaches the goal even at the low end: estimated reduction 31.4% to 46.3%. It costs up to $283,593 more than the budget, so meeting the goal may take more than the $800,000 set aside. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision once the gap is compared with the savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: As entered: P.S. 236 Langston Hughes (DOE building X173), 1871 Walton Avenue, Bronx; elementary school built 1994; 43,760 sq ft floor area; flat roof of 10,260 sq ft; annual electricity use 456,834 kWh (kWh is energy over time); utility Con Edison.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's energy report (Local Law 84, report year 2024) shows 456,834 kWh of electricity, the same as the entered figure, so it is treated as measured. Site energy use per square foot (EUI) is 57.6 kBtu (thousand BTU) per sq ft and the Energy Star score is 69.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's tax-lot record (tax lot number, or BBL, 2028510021) is listed under 1869 Walton Avenue, shows 4 floors, built 1994, and no landmark flag.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's building outline shows one building with a ground footprint of 10,255 sq ft, close to the 10,260 sq ft roof area entered. A footprint is the area under the building, not a measured roof, so the roof area is still the user's number and should be verified.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The user reports no existing efficiency work and no existing renewables, so the plan assumes none. The baseline for the goal is the electricity the building buys from the grid, which is 456,834 kWh a year.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Solar output range: system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around the 14% default of the PVWatts solar tool; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Usable roof is taken as 55% of the roof area, leaving room for edges, equipment and access paths.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Array density is 66 sq ft of usable roof for each kW of solar (kW is how much power at one moment).
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Battery size is an estimate: the critical load was not given, so it is taken as 1.0 W per sq ft over 43,760 sq ft, about 43.8 kW (not metered). The backup length was not given, so 8 hours is assumed. Battery energy is kW times hours divided by 0.85 round-trip efficiency, about 412 kWh.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency measures (LED lighting and controls) are assumed to save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Prices and savings percents behind every scenario are planning-level benchmarks, not quotes: solar $3,131-4,668 per kW and battery $546-812 per kWh (middle half of similar completed NYC projects, NYSERDA data); efficiency $1.17-4.02 per kWh saved a year (standard) and $1.09-3.83 (deep). The efficiency savings percents (10-20% standard, 15-25% deep) are planning estimates, and only 62%-88% of them is counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share (Local Law 87 report, DCAS, FY2022).
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Baseline: 456,834 kWh a year bought from the grid, measured (city energy report, 2024). Heating is not electric: the same report lists natural gas (893,000 kBtu) and fuel oil (69,276 kBtu), which an electricity goal does not cover.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Standard efficiency package (LED lighting and controls): planning estimate of 10-20% savings, with only 62%-88% of that counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share. Estimated reduction is 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, about 28,324 to 80,403 kWh a year.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Deeper efficiency package (Scenario C): planning estimate of 15-25% savings, with the same 62%-88% share counted. The trimmed share is not added back.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency cost: typical range $80,174 to $275,471 for the standard package; the median of similar NYC projects is about $175,424.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: No existing efficiency work is reported, so none was subtracted. The type of lighting now in place was not given. If lighting is already LED, the savings and the confidence in them would be lower.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Usable roof is about 5,643 sq ft (55% of 10,260 sq ft).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: That space fits an array of about 85.5 kW DC.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Estimated solar output is 101,100 to 111,098 kWh a year, with a central value of about 106,101 kWh, based on the PVWatts solar tool for this address.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: At the central output, solar covers about 23% of annual use. It does not reach the 30% goal by itself.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Solar bill savings are estimated at $20,028 to $26,864 a year (low output at the low price, high output at the high price), using the New York commercial average price of 19.8 to 24.2 cents per kWh. This is a statewide average, not the building's own tariff.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The city's roof assessment (Local Law 24) lists this roof as Not Solar Ready, in fair condition and 20 years or older. The roof may need repair or replacement before solar. None of the cost totals include roof work; a roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario A (efficiency only): reduction 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, which is 21% to 59% of the goal. It does not reach the goal. Typical cost range $80,174 to $275,471 (median of similar projects about $175,424); net cost is the same because no credit applies.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario A simple payback is 4.1 to 49.1 years (about 14 years at the median); this is a simple payback, not the full SAM model. Budget strain: within budget. Backup power: none, 0 outage hours.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B (standard efficiency plus 85.5 kW of solar, within budget): reduction 28.3% to 41.9% of annual use, which is 94% to 140% of the goal. It does not reach the goal at the low end. Typical upfront cost $347,875 to $674,585 (median about $487,585); net cost after the federal credit $267,565 to $554,851 (median about $393,937).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B simple payback is 5.8 to 21.6 years (about 11 years at the median). Budget strain: within budget, using 43% to 84% of $800,000. No backup power: solar panels shut off in an outage without a battery, so 0 outage hours.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C (deeper efficiency, whole-roof solar, 412 kWh battery): reduction 31.4% to 46.3% of annual use, which is 105% to 154% of the goal. It reaches the goal. Typical upfront cost $592,242 to $1,083,593 (median about $822,708); net cost after the federal credit $444,447 to $863,495 (median about $644,146).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C reaches the goal, but the estimated cost is up to $283,593 more than your budget. Reaching the goal may take more than the amount set aside; compare that gap with the savings before deciding whether to extend it. Budget strain: may exceed budget (74% to 135% of the budget).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C simple payback is 8.7 to 30.4 years (about 16.2 years at the median); this is a simple payback, not the full SAM model. Estimated annual bill savings are $28,444 to $51,165. Backup power covers about 8 to 9.4 hours.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: No surplus solar is expected, because the array is smaller than annual use. The budget is a capital amount, treated as one upfront total.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, standard-to-deep efficiency line: typical range $99,590 to $349,935; the median of similar NYC projects is about $227,503. Based on 91,367 kWh saved a year at $1.09-3.83 per kWh saved (middle half of completed NYC public-sector projects, NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C rooftop solar line: typical range $267,700 to $399,114; the median is about $312,160. Based on 85.5 kW at $3,131-4,668 per kW, the middle half of 558 completed NYC non-residential projects of 25-100 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data). This is real project data, not a quote.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C backup battery line: typical range $224,952 to $334,544; the median is about $283,044. Based on 412 kWh at $546-812 per kWh, the middle half of 56 completed or approved NYC commercial-scale storage projects (NYSERDA data). The battery is the largest reason Scenario C runs over budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C federal credit line: minus $147,796 to minus $220,097 (median about minus $178,561), 30% of solar and battery. The federal direct-pay credit for governmental entities was open when the page was read on 2026-10-19, but solar must be placed in service by 2027-12-31 and it is not confirmed here that this school or agency qualifies. Costs above are shown before the credit; net costs count it.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B federal credit line: minus $80,310 to minus $119,734 on the solar, with the same conditions on timing and eligibility.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: NY-Sun commercial solar incentive: status uncertain (the official dashboard could not be read automatically, retrieved 2026-10-19). Left out of net cost; check the dashboard in a browser.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: NYC Solar Schools program (DCAS, NYPA, NYC Public Schools, solar under power purchase agreements): status uncertain; 130 school installations are done, but it is not known whether this building is in the pipeline. Left out of net cost. Ask DCAS or the SCA, which could change the solar cost.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Roof repair or replacement is not in any total. A roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 0, confirm data and budget: confirm the 2027 capital budget and whether it is one total, check the electricity bills, confirm the tariff, and tell the planner what lighting and controls are already in place.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 1, professional reviews: a licensed structural PE or RA analysis and a roof condition survey before any solar, given the roof is 20 years or older and rated Not Solar Ready.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 2, efficiency measures: LED lighting and controls first, as they cost least and shrink the load.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 3, permits and interconnection: licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review, Department of Buildings permits and a Con Edison interconnection application, with DOE approval through DCAS, NYC Public Schools or the SCA.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 4, solar installation of about 85.5 kW only after the roof is cleared, aiming to be in service by 2027-12-31 so the federal credit may apply.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 5, battery, commissioning and checking results against bills. Decide on the battery after comparing the cost gap with the savings.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario C gives about 8 to 9.4 hours of backup for the critical loads, which are emergency lighting and communications.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenarios A and B give no backup power. Solar panels shut off in an outage without a battery.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The battery is sized from an estimated critical load of about 43.8 kW and an assumed 8 hours, not metered values; the real critical load and backup hours should be confirmed.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The current FEMA map shows flood zone X (minimal flood hazard) at this address. Heat and winter-storm ratings were not looked up, and the 2015 preliminary flood map was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The roof cannot be certified from these records. A licensed structural PE or RA must do the structural analysis, and a roof condition survey is needed (the roof is 20 years or older and not solar ready).
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Also required: a licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review and a Con Edison interconnection review. The list at the end of the plan has the links.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: This is a DOE building, so the approval route runs through DCAS, NYC Public Schools or the SCA.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: If the roof gets a major renovation, NYC's sustainable roof rule (Local Laws 92 and 94 of 2019) requires a solar system, a green roof, or both over the applicable roof.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city record shows no landmark flag, and the current flood map shows zone X, so no landmark or flood-zone review is added by these records.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Net-zero is not reached by this plan. Even the full path covers an estimated 31% to 46% of grid electricity, and heating still uses natural gas and fuel oil, which would need a separate electrification study.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The City's solar program for schools (130 installations so far) is the best learning resource and may offer a lower-cost route for this roof.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Confirm first: the city's tax-lot record is listed at 1869 Walton Avenue (the address asked was 1871) and gives a gross floor area of 46,700 sq ft, while the energy report and the entry show 43,760 sq ft. The entered 43,760 sq ft is the working figure. Please confirm.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Roof area is the user's number (10,260 sq ft) and the city outline shows 10,255 sq ft on the ground; an engineer or roofer should verify it. The year the roof was replaced was not given.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The electricity price is the New York commercial average, not this building's tariff. Con Edison lists several general-service tariffs (such as SC-2 and SC-9); the building's own tariff must be confirmed on a bill. Savings use the state average.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Incentive list: a person keeps this list and the system re-reads each official page. Two programs (NY-Sun and Solar Schools) came back uncertain and are left out of net cost. The federal credit was open but eligibility is not confirmed.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The flood-map service failed on the first try and worked on the second. Only the current flood zone was read; heat and storm ratings were not checked. Not provided: the type of lighting, cooling, controls, critical load, backup hours, owner confirmation and the user's own electricity price.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Confidence in cost and savings figures is low: the efficiency savings are planning estimates, the battery is sized from estimates, costs exclude the roof, and the payback is simple, not the full SAM model. No figure here is a promise of savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

roadmap.footer_note: All figures are estimates with ranges, not quotes. Savings cannot be guaranteed.
roadmap.plain_answer: You asked how P.S. 236 can cut the electricity it buys from the grid by 30% by 2030 on an $800,000 capital budget. The plan estimates that it can be done, but only with the full package: deeper efficiency work, solar on the whole roof and a backup battery. That package is estimated to cut 31% to 46% of your 456,834 kWh a year, and it costs between $592,242 and $1,083,593 before credits, so it could run up to $283,593 over your budget. A smaller package of standard efficiency plus solar fits the budget and is estimated to cut 28% to 42%, so it could fall just short of 30%. Solar alone covers only about 22% to 24% of your use. You have no solar or efficiency work in place today, so the baseline is all grid electricity. The roof is 20 years or older and the city lists it as not solar ready, and no cost here includes roof repair or replacement. Next steps: get a structural engineer and a roofer to review the roof, and confirm your bills and the federal credit with the city agencies that approve school work. All figures are estimates with ranges.
